questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presented with a 7-day history of cramping abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. She had opened her bowels over 15 times in the preceding 24 hours. There was fresh red blood mixed in with the stool. She had vomited once and felt feverish. Her symptoms had not abated since their onset. She had returned from a family holiday with her partner and three children 2 days before onset. Nobody else was symptomatic. She had no past medical history of note. Stool culture yielded Campylobacter jejuni.
questions.lead_in: In addition to fluid replacement therapy, what is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Azithromycin This is the first choice antibiotic for Campylobacter enteritis, as resistance is low for macrolide antibiotics.

questions.question: A man received an influenza vaccine 3 weeks ago and had an episode of acute gastroenteritis 1 week ago. He now presents with Guillain-Barre syndrome.
questions.question_raw: Man who got the flu shot 3 weeks ago, acute gastroenteritis 1 week ago. Now has GBS.

parts.text: What is the most likely reason for the Guillain-Barre syndrome?
Explain the pathophysiology of Guillain-Barre syndrome in this patient.

parts_raw.text: What is the most likely reason for GBS:
Explain the pathophysiology of GBS in this patient:

questions.model_answer:
a) Antecedent Campylobacter jejuni enteritis is the most likely cause. C. jejuni is the most important recognized antecedent of GBS, occurring at ~1 case per 2000 infections and typically 2-3 weeks after the diarrheal illness; the recent gastroenteritis fits far better than the influenza vaccine, whose attributable risk is very small.
b) Molecular mimicry. C. jejuni outer-membrane lipopolysaccharide/lipooligosaccharide carries sialic acid-containing structures that closely resemble human peripheral-nerve gangliosides (GM1, GD1a, GD3, GT1a). Infection elicits anti-glycolipid autoantibodies that cross-react with these ganglioside targets on peripheral nerves, producing immune-mediated nerve injury and flaccid paralysis. Particular strains (e.g., LPS serotype O:19) are over-represented among GBS cases.

cohort_answer.text: Most likely reason: Campylobacter jejuni infection (usually within 1-2 weeks post-infection); risk associated with influenza vaccine is very small. Pathophysiology: Molecular mimicry - Campylobacter contains ganglioside-like epitopes in the lipopolysaccharide moiety that elicit autoantibodies reacting with peripheral nerve targets.

questions.question: A previously well man presents with a subacute neurological picture of ascending weakness. He reports only mild diarrhea 6 weeks ago. His child recently arrived from Africa after receiving oral vaccines. (Alternate stem: a man who received an influenza vaccine 3 weeks ago and had acute gastroenteritis 1 week ago now has Guillain-Barre syndrome.)
questions.question_raw:
Q25 (2010 PM, 2014)
Complicated scenario in which patient presents with subacute neurological picture including ascending weakness. Mentions that he is otherwise well except for mild diarrhea 6 weeks ago. His child has recently come from Africa having been given oral vaccines.
Alternate stem: Man who got the flu shot 3 weeks ago, acute gastroenteritis 1 week ago, now has GBS.

parts.text: What is the most likely diagnosis and why?
Name one investigation to help confirm the diagnosis.
List four infectious causes of acute flaccid paralysis.
Explain the pathophysiology of Guillain-Barre syndrome in this patient.

parts_raw.text: A. What is most likely diagnosis and why?
B) One investigation to help confirm diagnosis?
C) 4 infectious causes of acute flaccid paralysis?
D) Explain the pathophysiology of GBS in this patient

questions.model_answer:
a) Guillain-Barre syndrome following Campylobacter jejuni enteritis. The antecedent diarrheal illness fits the recognized C. jejuni-GBS association (GBS usually 2-3 weeks post-infection; C. jejuni is the leading recognized antecedent). Argues against poliomyelitis: he is not from/exposed to a polio-endemic area, has no sick contacts, and sensory involvement with ascending weakness favours GBS over the pure motor picture of polio (oral polio vaccine in the child is a red herring).
b) Lumbar puncture showing albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF (raised protein with normal cell count); nerve conduction studies/EMG are also confirmatory.
c) (1) Poliovirus (poliomyelitis) (2) Non-polio enteroviruses (e.g., enterovirus D68, EV71) (3) West Nile virus (4) Corynebacterium diphtheriae (diphtheritic neuropathy). [C. jejuni-associated GBS is itself an additional infection-related cause.]
d) Molecular mimicry: C. jejuni LPS/lipooligosaccharide bears sialylated structures resembling human peripheral-nerve gangliosides (GM1, GD1a, GD3, GT1a). Cross-reactive autoantibodies generated against the organism attack these ganglioside epitopes on peripheral nerves; O:19 and certain capsular genotypes are over-represented in GBS.
questions.beyond_mandell: Parts b) and c) are not detailed in this Mandell chapter; CSF albuminocytologic dissociation/NCS and the list of infectious AFP causes (polio, enteroviruses, WNV, diphtheria) rest on standard neurology/CDC AFP knowledge.

cohort_answer.text:
A) Guillain-Barre syndrome secondary to Campylobacter gastroenteritis. No indication that the patient himself acquired a vector of a polio-like illness, nor were there sick contacts; no indication he was in an endemic region for polio (Afghanistan, Pakistan); sensory involvement would strongly indicate GBS vs polio.

B) CSF for albumin-cytologic dissociation. (Discussion: CSF classical findings seen in only 50% of patients; serial nerve conduction studies and EMG may be preferred. Albuminocytologic dissociation present in 50-66% of GBS patients in first week, ≥75% by third week; normal CSF protein found in 1/3-1/2 of patients tested earlier than 1 week and does not exclude GBS. NCS/EMG valuable for confirming diagnosis, prognosis, and classifying GBS as demyelinating vs axonal.)

C) WNV, Poliomyelitis, non-polio enteroviruses, Diphtheria.

D) Molecular mimicry - Campylobacter contains ganglioside-like epitopes in the lipopolysaccharide moiety that elicit autoantibodies reacting with peripheral nerve targets. Close resemblance of these sialylated structures to human gangliosides (GM1, GD1a, GD3, GT1a) and their presence in strains isolated from GBS patients supports a role in pathogenesis. Campylobacter outer membranes contain lipopolysaccharides (O-antigen) with endotoxic activity; O-antigens possess sialic acid-containing structures recognized by host immune cells with sialoadhesins, similar to human gangliosides.

parts.text: Micro 1 - microaerophilic, grows on charcoal-based selective media.

parts_raw.text: Micro 1 - microaerophilic, grows on charcoal something something
Micro 3 - NLF, catalase negative curved GNB

questions.model_answer: a) Campylobacter (e.g. C. jejuni) - microaerophilic, grows on charcoal- or blood-based selective media (Skirrow/CCDA) at 42 degrees C. b) Salmonella typhimurium - H2S producing (black colonies on XLD/Hektoen/SS agar), non-lactose fermenter. c) Vibrio cholerae - non-lactose fermenter, comma/curved gram-negative rod, oxidase-positive facultative anaerobe growing on TCBS/alkaline peptone water. d) Shigella sonnei - non-lactose (or late-lactose) fermenting, non-motile, biochemically inert enteric. Aeromonas is the unused distractor.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Vibrio descriptors (curved GNR, oxidase-positive, selective media) are in this chapter; the Campylobacter, Salmonella, and Shigella identifications rest on standard clinical microbiology (Mandell species chapters / Manual of Clinical Microbiology).

questions.question_raw:
Q41 (2013 AM)
Stool pathogens, various microbiological features, match pathogen to features. Micro features given: Microaerophilic grows on charcoal; H2S producing NLF, catalase negative (maybe oxidase negative) curved GNB; NLF catalase negative (may be oxidase negative). Organisms: Vibrio, Shigella sonnei, Salmonella typhimurium, Campylobacter, Aeromonas

parts.text: Match each pathogen to its microbiological features.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Microaerophilic, grows on charcoal = Campylobacter (spiral/vibrioid gram-negative rod, thermophilic 42 C, oxidase and catalase positive, requires microaerobic incubation and selective/charcoal media). (2) H2S-producing non-lactose fermenter = Salmonella typhimurium (facultatively anaerobic Enterobacteriaceae, oxidase-negative, produces H2S). (3) Non-lactose fermenter, catalase-negative/oxidase-negative = Shigella sonnei (nonmotile, no H2S). Vibrio and Aeromonas are oxidase-positive non-lactose fermenters and do not fit these three cues.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Campylobacter microbiology (microaerophilic, charcoal/selective media, oxidase/catalase-positive vibrioid morphology) is from this chapter; the Salmonella, Shigella, Vibrio and Aeromonas features rest on standard clinical microbiology (Manual of Clinical Microbiology).

cohort_answer.text: Microaerophilic grows on charcoal - Campylobacter. H2S producing NLF, catalase negative (maybe oxidase negative) curved GNB - Salmonella. NLF catalase negative (may be oxidase negative) - Shigella. Additional detail: Vibrio - gram negative, non-lactose fermenter, curved-rod (comma) shape, facultative anaerobe, oxidase positive, motile with polar flagella. Shigella sonnei - nonmotile, facultatively anaerobic GNR, non-lactose fermenter, no H2S, indole positive, ferments glucose/urea, oxidase negative, differentiated by ornithine decarboxylase expression. Salmonella typhimurium - gram negative facultatively anaerobic Enterobacteriaceae, non-lactose fermenter, oxidase negative, produces H2S. Campylobacter - spiral shape, long flagella, mostly microaerophilic, thermophilic, nonfermentative, oxidase and catalase positive, urease negative (vs Helicobacter urease positive). Aeromonas - gram negative, non-lactose fermenter, oxidase positive, ferments glucose
